segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, since you know that we will receive a stricter judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we guide their whole body as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look at ships too: though they are so large and are driven by harsh winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the helmsman's impulse directs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So too the tongue is a small part of the body, and it boasts of great things. See how small a fire kindles how great a forest!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is set among the parts of our body as the world of unrighteousness; it stains the whole body, sets ablaze the wheel of existence, and is itself set ablaze by Gehenna.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the tongue no human being can tame: a restless evil, full of deadly poison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people, who have been made in the likeness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers and sisters, these things ought not to be so.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Does a spring gush sweet and bitter water from the same opening?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Can a fig tree, my brothers and sisters, produce olives, or a grapevine figs? Neither can salt water produce sweet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show his works by his good way of life, in the gentleness of wisdom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This wisdom is not the kind that comes down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there is disorder and every base deed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peaceable, forbearing, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without pretense.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, not males only. James is writing to whole congregations, so 'brothers and sisters' gives what the first readers would have heard. Many recent translations do the same; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

Some manuscripts read 'Look' (ide) instead of 'Now if' (ei de); the two were pronounced almost identically in this period. The older English tradition followed the first reading. Most modern editions prefer 'Now if', and the sense is little affected.

The grammar and punctuation of this verse are notoriously difficult. The phrase may describe the tongue (it stands among the body's parts as the unrighteous world in miniature), or it may be attached to 'fire' in the previous clause. A minority take the word in its other sense, 'adornment', meaning that the tongue makes wrongdoing attractive. The rendering here follows the most common reading.

notes.traditional: the course of nature / the whole course of life
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'the wheel of birth' or 'of becoming'. Similar phrases appear in Greek religious and philosophical writing for the cycle of life, and by this period the image seems to have been a general expression for the whole round of human existence. Most translations paraphrase as 'the course of life'. Keeping 'wheel' preserves the image, though exactly what James had in mind is uncertain.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the Jewish term for the place of final fiery judgment. 'Hell' merges it with Hades and with later imagery, so the name is kept. Many translations still use 'hell', usually with a footnote giving Gehenna.
The phrase echoes the Greek version of Genesis 1:26, where humanity is made 'according to our image and likeness'. The point is that cursing a person insults the God whose likeness that person bears.

'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive manner, here set against the jealousy and ambition of the next verse. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the mainstream modern rendering.

This word is rare outside the New Testament. Its earlier attested use is for self-seeking pursuit of position, which supports 'selfish ambition', the choice of most modern translations. Older versions connected it with a similar-looking word for strife and rendered it 'strife' or 'contention'. Some scholars prefer 'rivalry' or 'party spirit'.

The adjective comes from the word for 'soul' or 'life' and describes what belongs to ordinary human life as opposed to what comes from God's Spirit. 'Natural' is the more literal alternative, but in modern English that sounds like praise. The older 'sensual' wrongly suggests bodily appetite.

The word describes someone reasonable and fair, who does not insist on the full letter of their rights. It is usually translated 'gentle'. Here it is kept distinct from the different Greek word rendered 'gentleness' in verse 13. 'Considerate' and 'reasonable' are other common renderings.

The word can mean 'making no distinctions', which gives 'impartial', or 'undivided, unwavering'. The related verb is used in both ways in this letter, for doubting in 1:6 and for discriminating between people in 2:4. Translators and commentators are divided; the second option would give 'unwavering'.

The Greek can equally mean 'for those who make peace', so that the peacemakers are the ones who benefit from the harvest and not those who sow it. 'The fruit of righteousness' may also mean either the fruit that consists of righteousness or the fruit that righteousness produces. Most translations choose 'by', as here.

candidates.reason: The plural address occurs throughout the letters, and translators split between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'; readers will notice if it varies between chapters.
It recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, where 'perfect', 'mature' and 'complete' are all defensible and inconsistent choices would obscure links between passages.
It occurs here, in 1 Corinthians 2 and 15, and in Jude 19, with 'natural', 'unspiritual', 'worldly' and 'sensual' all in use, and the contrast with 'spiritual' should be visible consistently.
It is usually rendered 'gentle', which collides with the register's 'gentle' for πραΰς; it needs its own fixed rendering across Philippians, the Pastorals, James and 1 Peter.
The word covers both commendable zeal and destructive jealousy or envy across many books, and a rule on how to divide the senses in English would keep chapters consistent.
